questions.concept: Field as a property of space
questions.question: Why do we say a charge creates an 'electric field' around it, rather than just saying it exerts forces on other charges?
questions.solution: The field concept localises the influence: the charge modifies the space around it, and any charge ENTERING that space feels a force — no action-at-a-distance delay or mystery needed. E = F/q₀ gives the force per unit test charge at each point. Fields also carry energy and momentum, which the bare 'force' picture hides.

questions.question: Why can two electric field lines never intersect?
questions.solution: The tangent to a field line at a point gives the direction of E there. If two lines crossed, E would have two directions at one point — impossible, since the force on a test charge is unique. Crossing would mean the field is double-valued; the rule is a logical consequence of the definition.

questions.question: Why does an electric dipole's field fall as 1/r³ while a single charge's falls as 1/r²?
questions.solution: A dipole is two equal and opposite charges very close together: at large distance their 1/r² fields nearly cancel, and what survives is the small DIFFERENCE between the two — a next-order term falling as 1/r³. Cancellation promotes the field to a faster decay. The same logic makes the quadrupole fall as 1/r⁴.

questions.question: A dipole sits in a uniform electric field. What is the net force and the net torque on it?
questions.solution: Net force is zero: +q and −q feel equal and opposite forces in a uniform field. Net torque τ = pE sinθ is nonzero unless the dipole aligns with E — the torque rotates the dipole toward alignment, doing work stored as potential energy U = −pE cosθ. Uniform field: no translation, only rotation.

questions.question: Why is the electric field zero everywhere inside a charged hollow conducting sphere?
questions.solution: In electrostatic equilibrium the charges reside on the outer surface and redistribute until the field inside each conductor point is zero — otherwise free electrons would keep moving. Gauss's law confirms it: any Gaussian surface inside encloses zero net charge, so flux — and by symmetry, field — is zero. This shielding is why electronics are boxed in metal.
